title: KV prefetch window sensitivity notes
content:
Context / motivation:
This note collects exploratory results and hypotheses from a small lab sprint focused on how the 'prefetch window' parameter interacts with long-tail reuse patterns and memory bandwidth on our A100-class nodes. We observed two customer incidents where tail latency spiked under mixed seqlen workloads; both correlated with heavy background paging and an increase in NVMe IO. The goal here is pragmatic: find safe ranges for the prefetch window (lookahead pages / KV segments) that improve reuse without triggering bank saturation or spillback oscillation.

Executive summary (high level):
- Small prefetch windows (1-2 pages) reduce NVMe IO but miss medium-term reuse (20–200 reqs) causing extra host-to-device transfers.
- Large windows (>8 pages) catch more reuse but increase simultaneous read amplification and memory channel contention — we saw up to 1.6x DRAM bandwidth usage and localized NVMe bursts that increased tail latency for other tenant classes.
- A dynamic window that reduces prefetch width under sustained bank queueing keeps 95/99p latency stable while preserving hit-rate gains.

Hypotheses tested:
1) Prefetching contiguous pages improves token-level reuse for transformer workloads with moderate prefix overlap, but only up to the point where device memory bandwidth becomes the limiting factor.
2) The marginal reuse benefit of expanding the prefetch window decays exponentially with window size; cost (bandwidth + eviction churn) grows superlinearly.
3) A short stabilization delay (50–200ms of observing bank queue depth) before expanding the window prevents oscillation and reduces spillback.

Experiment design / configuration:
- Hardware: 2 x A100-40GB nodes (single tenant isolated tests), NVMe SSD per node; kernel/perf counters collected via bpftrace and nvme-cli traces.
- Runtime: internal dev build with prefetch parameter exposed: PREFETCH_WINDOW_PAGES (1,2,4,8,12) and PREFETCH_DELAY_MS (0,50,200).
- Workloads: three synthetic mixes plus a sampled production trace replay.
  - Mix A (chatty short): 70% seqlen<64, 30% seqlen 256, moderate prefix overlap (avg reuse window 30 requests).
  - Mix B (document retrieval): many long requests seqlen 512+, low prefix overlap.
  - Mix C (mixed enterprise): 40% short, 40% medium (128–256), 20% long, heavy concurrency (QPS scaled up until small tail latency degradation observed).
  - Trace: 2 hours of sampled requests from region-us-west (redacted keys) with observed NVMe activity in production spikes.

Metrics collected (textual):
- KV hit rate (per-request and aggregated per-token).
- NVMe read IO ops/sec and read throughput (MB/s).
- DRAM/channel bandwidth (sampled via nvprof/perf counters): overall and per-memory-channel where possible.
- Eviction churn: pages evicted per second and average resident lifetime.
- Latency: p50/p95/p99 for token generation and full request completion.

Key results (selected):
- Mix A:
  - Window=1: KV hit 0.38, NVMe read 950 ops/s, p99 token latency 220ms.
  - Window=4: KV hit 0.61, NVMe read 780 ops/s, p99 token latency 200ms. (improvement)
  - Window=12: KV hit 0.66, NVMe read 1800 ops/s, p99 token latency 420ms. (regression due to bandwidth peaks)
- Mix B:
  - Window scaling had marginal effect on hit rate (0.12 -> 0.18) but increased NVMe MB/s linearly; prefetch wasted many cold pages. Avoid big windows for low-overlap workloads.
- Mix C:
  - Window=4 with PREFETCH_DELAY_MS=200 stabilized p99 at 280ms and NVMe reads at moderate levels (1.1x baseline).
  - Window=8 with no delay produced oscillation: periodic NVMe bursts, eviction spikes, and p99 spikes >700ms every ~90s.
- Trace replay:
  - Dynamic-window prototype (start=2, expand to max 6 with delay) reduced average NVMe ops by 30% relative to static window=8 while keeping p95 within 5% of optimal.

Observations / interpretation:
- There is a clear tradeoff: bigger prefetch windows are helpful when reuse locality exists and request concurrency is moderate. But when concurrency pushes memory channel utilization, read amplification from prefetching triggers evictions and repeated spillback which exacerbate tail latency.
- The marginal gain curve: most reuse benefits occur moving from 1->4 pages. After 4, hit-rate improvements are small but bandwidth costs grow faster. This suggests a conservative default of 2–4 pages for multi-tenant/shared nodes.
- Delaying aggressive expansion until the runtime sees a low bank queue depth prevents the synchronized expansion across shards that causes bursts. In other words, the control loop should be bank-aware and slightly damped.
- Cold-heavy workloads (Mix B) show prefetching is net negative; we should fall back to demand-loading for low-overlap signals.

Runtime telemetry correlation examples (notes):
- When NVMe read latency climbs for >200ms and DRAM channel saturation >75%, eviction rate doubles; this quickly eats into any hit-rate gains from larger windows.
- In one test we saw prefetch threads launch 512KB reads concurrently across channels; resulting PCIe traffic caused CPU stalls in the host-side prefetch queue which cascaded to request scheduling jitter.

Recommendations (operational and product):
1) Default PREFETCH_WINDOW_PAGES=2 with initial quick warmup (aggressive for first 20ms) and then conservative expansion up to 4 pages under healthy bank conditions.
2) Implement bank_queue_depth signal as a first-class metric; if above threshold (per-card) block further window expansion and backoff prefetching rate.
3) For low-overlap workloads detect via recent reuse histogram (low per-request reuse in last N requests) and switch to demand-loading mode (no prefetch). Flag tunables to Dedicated customers.
4) Add an adaptive stabilization timer (configurable: 50–250ms) to avoid synchronized multi-shard expansion.
5) Add runtime telemetry that explicitly correlates prefetch read amplification (pages pulled / token served) with eviction churn so we can build automated guardrails.

Small prototype to ship (MVP):
- Runtime switches: PREFETCH_WINDOW_MIN, PREFETCH_WINDOW_MAX, PREFETCH_DELAY_MS, BANK_BACKOFF_THRESHOLD.
- Telemetry: prefetch_pages_pulled, prefetch_backoff_events, bank_queue_depth.
- Safety: if eviction_rate > X and NVMe_iops > Y over sliding window -> force PREFETCH_WINDOW=1 for 10s.

Open questions and follow-ups:
- Is per-tenant or per-shard prefetch control necessary, or can a single card-level control suffice? (We will test mixed-tenant experiments next.)
- Does dynamic quantization/pinned memory interaction change threshold behaviors? Haven't tested with int8 / q4 profiles yet.
- How well do the lab results map to other HW (L40s, older V100 successors)? Need cross-hardware sweep.
- Can we design a cheap ML classifier (tiny logistic) to predict when prefetch is counterproductive using 10 runtime features? Worth exploring in a later sprint.

Experiment TODOs / action items:
- [ ] Run mixed-tenant scenario: 2 tenants with opposite patterns (one cold-heavy, one chatty) and measure fairness impact (owner: Marek). Due: 2024-09-01.
- [ ] Add bank_queue_depth metric to observability backend + dashboard (Sofia). Due: 2024-08-28.
- [ ] Implement PREFETCH_DELAY_MS throttle in prototype branch and run 24h stability replay (Devon). Due: 2024-09-04.
- [ ] Sweep across quantization profiles on small scale (Aisha). Due: 2024-09-10.

Quick notes to self (informal):
- Watch out for synchronized timers: if shards all use same heuristic window, they expand in lockstep and create periodic bursts. Try staggered seeds per-shard.
- When writing PR, include microbench that reproduces bandwidth spike deterministically; easier to test guardrail.

References / links:
- Jira: JIRA-RT-1423 (investigation ticket)
- Prototype PR: github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/879
- Related runbook: paging-cost-and-operational-guide (confluence link TBD)

Concluding remark:
This sprint produced actionable heuristics: small default window, bank-aware expansion, and a fallback to demand-loading for low-overlap workloads. Next step is to harden telemetry and validate multi-tenant fairness.

-- Aisha
